Company: Brightside Foods Co.

US mid-size packaged food company (~900 employees, plants in Ohio and Georgia). Makes hot dogs and sausages, brightly colored gummy candy, and pecan-and-apple snack bars. Buys pecans, apples and corn from US farms. Sells through grocery chains and convenience stores (many customers pay with SNAP / food stamps). Runs its own fleet of 40 delivery trucks. No restaurants, no alcohol, no exports.

Rules that APPLY:
- FDA food additive and color additive rules (dyes in candy, casings, meat)
- Food labeling and food safety rules for packaged food and meat products
- EPA pesticide residue limits on crops we buy (pecans, apples, corn)
- USDA marketing orders and grading for pecans and apples
- SNAP rules that change what shoppers can buy or who qualifies (affects demand)
- Workplace safety and labor rules for food plants; trucking safety rules for our fleet

Rules that DO NOT apply:
- Aviation, airspace, aircraft airworthiness
- Banking, securities, crypto, sanctions
- Medicare/Medicaid payment rules, medical devices
- Mining, offshore oil and gas, fisheries
- Broadcast/TV licensing

Abstract: The Surface Transportation Board (STB or Board) is issuing this policy statement on the scope of its jurisdiction over transportation by rail carriers and on preemption of conflicting state and federal laws under the ICC Termination Act of 1995 (ICCTA). [2026-22865] Rule — Health and Human Services Department; Food and Drug Administration
Title: Color Additive Petition From Environmental Defense Fund et al.; Request To Amend the Color Additive Regulations To Remove the Solvents Ethylene Dichloride, Methylene Chloride, and Trichloroethylene
Action: Final amendment; order; notification of partial denial of petition.
Abstract: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or we) is partially granting a color additive petition submitted by Environmental Defense Fund et al. (petitioners), by amending our color additive regulations, on the basis of the Delaney Clause, to remove the authorized use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. The petitioners provided data demonstrating that this additive induces cancer in laboratory animals. We are denying the remaining petition requests to remove ethylene dichloride, methylene chloride, and trichloroethylene from the list of authorized extraction solvents for annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin, because any residue of the solvent would be an impurity in the color additive and such impurities are not subject to the Delaney Clause.

[2026-22866] Rule — Health and Human Services Department; Food and Drug Administration
Title: Color Additive Petition From the International Association of Color Manufacturers; Request To Amend the Color Additive Regulations To Remove the Solvents Methylene Chloride, Trichloroethylene, and Ethylene Dichloride
Action: Final amendment; order; notification of partial denial of petition.
Abstract: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or we) is partially granting a color additive petition submitted by the International Association of Color Manufacturers (IACM or petitioner), by amending our color additive regulations, on the basis of abandonment, to remove the authorized uses of methylene chloride, trichloroethylene, and ethylene dichloride from the list of authorized extraction solvents for annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, and turmeric oleoresin. The petitioner provided data demonstrating that these uses have been permanently abandoned. FDA is denying as moot the portion of the petition proposing that the color additive regulations be amended, on the basis of abandonment, to no longer authorize the use of methylene chloride as a diluent in color additive mixtures in inks for marking fruit and vegetables. This request is moot because the authorization for this use has been removed, on the basis of the Delaney Clause, in response to a separate petition.

[2026-22903] Proposed Rule — Labor Department; Employment and Training Administration
Title: Unemployment Insurance Program National Minimum Weekly Work Search Requirements
Action: Proposed rule, request for comment.
Abstract: The U.S. Department of Labor (Department), through the Employment and Training Administration (ETA), is proposing to amend 20 CFR part 604 both to reflect a 2012 update in Federal law in which Congress, by amending section 303(a) of the Social Security Act (SSA), established a Federal work search requirement; and to establish a national minimum weekly work search requirement standard for the Federal-State unemployment compensation (UC) program. This proposed rule would mandate, among other things, that States require individuals claiming UC to complete at least five qualifying work search activities or, where applicable, meet State-adopted points-based system requirements amounting to five qualifying activities or satisfy equivalent labor force attachment criteria, each week for which UC is claimed; that individuals report their work search activities as part of their certification process prior to payment being issued; and that State law allow for certain qualifying work search activities beyond simply employer contacts. This action is necessary to reduce inconsistencies beyond those created by local labor markets in State- level requirements for individuals to actively seek work.

[2026-22936] Proposed Rule — Agriculture Department; Food and Nutrition Administration
Title: Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility
Action: Proposed rule.
Abstract: Under section 5(a) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, households in which each member receives benefits under a State program funded by Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) are categorically eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Current SNAP regulations consider TANF benefits to include both cash assistance and non-cash or in-kind benefits or services from TANF-funded programs. This proposal would limit categorical eligibility to only households that receive TANF assistance, as defined at 45 CFR 260.31. These revisions would ensure that SNAP benefits are targeted to needy households that have qualified for TANF assistance while still aligning categorical eligibility's statutory purpose of simplifying program administration. A 100-word summary of this rule has been posted to www.regulations.gov and can be found here.

markdown:
# Regulatory triage — Brightside Foods Co.
Window 2026-11-09 → 2026-11-13 · as of 2026-11-13 · 5 items

## Critical (4)

- **Pecans Grown in the States of Alabama, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, New Mexico, Oklahoma, South Carolina, and Texas; Changes to Membership and Handling Requirements** [Federal Register]
  - Review the proposed pecan marketing order changes with Georgia suppliers and submit comments if new late fees, handler reporting duties, or council changes would raise our pecan costs.
  - Dates: comment 2026-12-09 ✓ · Owner: Tom Alvarez (Sourcing) · Areas: sourcing
  - 91 FR 70809 ✓ · https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/09/2026-22826/pecans-grown-in-the-states-of-alabama-arkansas-arizona-california-florida-georgia-kansas-louisiana
- **Color Additive Petition From the International Association of Color Manufacturers; Request To Amend the Color Additive Regulations To Remove the Solvents Methylene Chloride, Trichloroethylene, and Ethylene Dichloride** [Federal Register]
  - Ask color suppliers whether their annatto, paprika and turmeric extracts use the solvents being removed, and comment if reformulation could disrupt gummy or sausage supply.
  - Dates: comment 2026-12-10 ✓ · effective 2027-01-11 ✓ · Owner: Maria Chen (Food Safety & Regulatory) · Areas: food-safety, sourcing
  - 91 FR 72410 ✓ · https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/10/2026-22866/color-additive-petition-from-the-international-association-of-color-manufacturers-request-to-amend
- **Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program: Reforming Categorical Eligibility** [Federal Register]
  - Estimate how much of our sales depends on SNAP shoppers losing eligibility under this proposal, and decide whether to file comments on expected demand impact.
  - Dates: comment 2026-12-10 ✓ · Owner: Aisha Grant (Sales Compliance) · Areas: sales
  - 91 FR 72454 ✓ · https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/10/2026-22936/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-reforming-categorical-eligibility
- **Modification to Work Requirements for Able-Bodied Adults** [Federal Register]
  - Assess how tighter SNAP work requirements could reduce customer purchases of our products, and decide whether to submit comments with sales data showing the impact.
  - Dates: comment 2026-12-10 ✓ · Owner: Aisha Grant (Sales Compliance) · Areas: sales
  - 91 FR 72439 ✓ · https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/10/2026-22944/modification-to-work-requirements-for-able-bodied-adults

## High (1)

- **Revocation of the Color Additive Listing for Use of Orange B on Casings or Surfaces of Frankfurters and Sausages; Confirmation of Effective Date** [Federal Register]
  - Confirm no hot dog or sausage casings use Orange B color, and verify supplier certifications and labels so no noncompliant product ships.
  - Dates: other 2026-08-24 ✓ · effective 2026-09-08 ✓ · Owner: Maria Chen (Food Safety & Regulatory) · Areas: food-safety, operations
  - 91 FR 73139 ✓ · https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/11/13/2026-23112/revocation-of-the-color-additive-listing-for-use-of-orange-b-on-casings-or-surfaces-of-frankfurters

votes.why: Plain language with a concrete step: review the changes with Georgia suppliers and comment if costs rise.
Calls the changes proposed and names only late fees, reporting and council changes; it does not claim quality, size or price standards change.
Mentions the proposed marketing order changes, including late fees, and their effect on Georgia pecan suppliers.
Clear step: ask color suppliers about solvent use and comment if supply could be disrupted.
Says only the solvents are being removed, not that the colors are banned or unsafe.
Conveys that solvents used to extract annatto, paprika and turmeric are being removed and says to check suppliers.
Understandable step: estimate SNAP-dependent sales exposure, then decide whether to comment.
Refers to it as a proposal and claims no food purchase restrictions.
Conveys a proposal under which shoppers lose eligibility and the resulting impact on sales.
Clear step: assess the purchase impact and decide whether to comment with sales data.
Does not claim the rule is final or that it restricts which foods SNAP can buy; the comment option implies it is a proposal.
Mentions tighter SNAP work requirements (proposed status implied by the comment step) and reduced product purchases.
Concrete step: confirm casings contain no Orange B and verify supplier certifications and labels.
Does not call the revocation proposed and limits it to hot dog and sausage casings.
Conveys that Orange B is not allowed on casings and calls for checking suppliers.
The owner has a concrete first step: review the changes with Georgia suppliers to see whether they could raise pecan costs.
It describes the changes as proposed and treats higher costs as a possibility, not as a change to price standards.
It identifies the proposed pecan marketing order changes, including late fees, and connects them to the company's Georgia pecan suppliers and sourcing costs.
It gives the owner a concrete question to ask color suppliers: whether they use the solvents in the three named extracts.
It distinguishes the solvents from the colors and treats reformulation and supply disruption as possibilities.
It conveys that certain extraction solvents are being removed for the three natural colors and directs the owner to check whether suppliers use them.
The wording makes it sound as though sales depend on shoppers losing eligibility, rather than asking how much the company sells to shoppers who could lose eligibility.
It frames eligibility loss as a consequence of a proposal and makes no claim that the rule is in effect or limits eligible foods.
Despite the awkward phrasing, it links the proposal to shoppers losing SNAP eligibility and puts the company's sales to those shoppers under review.
It plainly asks the owner to assess how tighter SNAP work requirements could affect purchases of the company's products.
It treats lower sales as a possible effect and does not claim the rule is final or changes what shoppers can buy.
The action and comment date convey that tighter SNAP work requirements are proposed and could reduce purchases of the company's products.
It gives the owner a concrete compliance check: use supplier records and labels to verify that casings contain no Orange B.
The casing check follows from the revocation and does not imply that Orange B is banned in other foods.
It covers casing checks and supplier verification but misses Orange B applied directly to hot dog or sausage surfaces.
Plain English giving a concrete review-and-comment step for the sourcing owner.
Supported by the title and reason, and avoids claiming the rule is final or alters quality/price standards.
Mentions proposed pecan marketing order changes including late fees and handler reporting, and connects them to pecan suppliers/costs.
Clear, plain-English instruction to check with color suppliers and comment if needed.
Supported by the reason and title, and does not claim the colors themselves are banned or unsafe.
Conveys that solvents for annatto, paprika, and turmeric extracts are being removed and instructs asking color suppliers if they use them.
Plain English naming a concrete sales-impact estimation and comment decision.
Accurately reflects a proposed rule affecting eligibility without claiming finality or food restrictions.
Conveys proposed SNAP eligibility loss and potential reduction in company sales.
Plain-English instruction to assess impact and decide on submitting comments.
Supported by the title, reason, and comment date, and avoids prohibited claims.
Covers tighter SNAP work requirements (with comment context showing it is proposed) and potential reduction in product purchases.
Clear, plain-English action to confirm compliance and check supplier certifications and labels.
Fully supported by the title and reason, and avoids claiming it is only proposed or applies to candy.
Conveys that Orange B on hot dog/sausage casings is noncompliant and instructs verifying supplier certifications.
